text:
The fault is most likely an undersized tail transistor M5, which leaves the M5/M6 mirror delivering too little tail current. M6 is the close alternative.

**What the numbers show**

- **Tail current.** M6 carries the 10 µA reference. M5 mirrors it at W ratio 3.436/1.139 ≈ 3, so the tail is about 30 µA and each input device gets about 15 µA.
- **UGBW from input gm.** The input transistors run at gm/Id ≈ 21.3, so gm ≈ 325 µS. Then gm / (2π · 2 pF) ≈ 26 MHz, which matches the simulated 24.7 MHz.
- **What the spec needs.** Reaching 43 MHz needs roughly 1.7× more gm. Since gm/Id is already near its weak-inversion ceiling, that has to come from about 1.7× more current, i.e. a tail of around 50 µA. That corresponds to a mirror ratio of about 5 rather than 3.
- **Settling.** Slew is 30 µA / 2 pF ≈ 15 V/µs, which is too slow for 33 ns settling. This points to the same cause.
- **What still works.** Gain, phase margin and polarity all pass, so the signal path and the load mirror (M3/M4) are intact. Only the tail bias level is wrong.

**Why M5 rather than M6**

The fault could be either M5 being too narrow or M6 being too wide, and both give the same mirror ratio. The sensitivities point the same way: ugbw rises 18% when M5 grows and falls 16% when M6 grows. I rank M5 first because a shrunk tail device is the more common corruption. M5 and M6 share the same Vgs and L, so their Vdsat does not separate the two cases. The input pair (M1) is a distant third.
